An AI "hallucination" in a court filing is a citation, quotation or proposition of law generated by an AI tool that does not exist or does not say what the filing claims. Since [[mata-v-avianca]] in 2023, courts around the world have reported hundreds of such incidents, involving lawyers and self-represented litigants alike. Public trackers, such as the database maintained by researcher Damien Charlotin, catalogue them.

## How courts respond

Responses range from warnings to monetary sanctions, fee awards, disqualification and referrals to disciplinary authorities, as in [[johnson-v-dunn]]. Courts consistently say the problem is not the use of AI but the failure to verify. Many judges now require certifications about AI use in filings.

## Outside the United States

Judges and bar bodies elsewhere have issued similar warnings, including guidance in England and Wales and Canada and, in October 2026, public remarks by a retired Nigerian Supreme Court justice urging lawyers to verify AI-generated citations.

## Insurance angle

Sanctions are often uninsurable, but the incident can trigger a client malpractice claim and disciplinary defense costs. See [[lawyers-professional-liability-and-ai]].
